raw_comment:
I notice that the highest percentile of the soil moisture was around the near 1990s up until the 2000s. 
I wonder why the soil moisture percentile drops so much and so fast after we hit the 2000s.
It relates to me because I live in Socal where we have been in a drought for the longest since the 2000s. It affects the community because it makes the water bill go up even higher and also makes everyone complain about the weather. 
¨Stop and Save Water. Living in Hot Times¨

raw_comment: The first thing I noticed looking at this graph was the pattern that exists very generally throughout the graph; following a drought always comes a wet period of around the same "magnitude". This can be observed in the megadrought occurring from 1572-1600. It appears that prior to that megadrought, there was a period of 75th+ percentile soil moisture, and directly after the megadrought was another one. It leads me to wonder why that occurs. Given that there is currently a megadrought in the Southwest, will there be a period over the next 50 or so years where the soil moisture is over the 75th percentile? Ultimately, I wonder if this 21st-century megadrought will be worse, or last longer than the one from 1572-1600.

raw_comment:
We noticed an oscillation between wet and dry periods - while the droughts stand out, they are often preceded by periods of wet.  The graphs also look like the inside of a cave, with stalactites and stalagmites!

Between the 1700s and 1800s there were no big changes, but more of a general drought.

We initially wondered what caused the megadrought in 1572 but did some research and discovered that it may have been caused by ocean currents similar to El Nino/La Nina

This can relate to our community because we are also currently in drought conditions (and also feel like Texas should have been considered in the southwest region).

Our title is Mega Drought: No Doubt

raw_comment:
1. What do I notice?  
This graph highlights a variation of the data collected from past and present drought throughout the Southwest. The graph displays evidence dating back to the 1500s, allowing a far range of data. It is noticeable that the waves of drought come in and out throughout the years. Some years there is no drought, while others there is much more drought. 
What do I wonder? 
I wonder what happened during 1572-1600 that could have caused such an intense and longlasting drought. I wonder if it will repeat in the future. 
What do I think is going on in this graph? 
This graph displays a wave of dry and wet times throughout history. What is going on is that there are times of extreme dry, as well as times of extreme wetness. 
How does this relate to you and your community?
Droughts can happen all over the world, at any time. It is important to understand and recognize when and where droughts have occurred in places other than my community because it could tell us something about the history of our drought as well. 
Headline: Waves of drought throughout the Southwest

raw_comment:
This graph shows the history of droughts in the Southwest from around the year 1500 to present day. Orange and dark brown represent the least moisture, while darker green represents the most moisture. It seems as though the biggest droughts occurred in the 16th and17th centuries, especially between 1572 and 1600. In between those extreme droughts, however, were extreme wet periods. There is also an extreme drought happening currently. The graph shows less extremes, whether periods of moisture or drought, from the 1700s-2000s. The ever-changing status of the drought is likely related to change in season. 
I wonder how indicative droughts are of climate change and when droughts in the United States started to bring attention to changes in the climate. 
My community is not experiencing an extreme drought as the local governments have not given any warning or advised against excessive water use. 
A headline for this graph would be "It Was Supposed to Rain... Must have 'Mist' Us!"

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
From about the mid-1600s to 1900 the moisture of the soil has been fairly consistent. However, before and after the late 1500s megadrought there were periods of an extremely wet soil, and there has been similar extreme climate periods since 1900, and they are worse than ever before. Currently the soil is the driest it's ever been. The current megadrought has not lasted as long as the late 1500s one, and it doesn't seem like it's going to stop soon.
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder what other environmental changes were happening during the last megadrought, and if there were other extreme things happening in nature like climate change now. I also wonder why periods of extreme wetness and extreme dryness follow each other.
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
Climate change affects all of us, because if things continue as they are we soon won't have a world to live in. It's also very difficult for individuals to do anything about climate change, so it's disheartening to see these terrible effects and know most of us can't do much about them.
4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
The Future is Dry

raw_comment:
I notice that the places on the graph that have super high amounts of dark brown (driest) are surrounded by a lot of dark green (wettest). I also notice that the current megadrought is the highest percentage since (and a higher than) the megadrought from 1572-1600. 
I wonder what this graph will look like moving forward and if the current drought going on is completely unprecedented or if its expected in the natural cycle of the land (since the last megadrought was close to 400 years ago, is it expected that another one would be happening now?).
This graph, and the droughts going on around the country, makes me glad I live in a place that has a lot of fresh water.

raw_comment:
I notice that in 2000 the southwest was the wettest, but in 22 years there was a very sharp turnaround and now we are entering a megadrought, which seems to last around 30 years.

I wonder if the megadrought we are entering is part of a regular cycle of droughts and wet periods, or if this one will be more permanent due to climate change, and if the data can tell us this.

It relates to me as this drought as well as climate change in general will be affecting my generation as we grow up, and we will be the ones facing the more long term consequences of the drought.

My title would be "Megadroughts Cause Mega Pouts!

raw_comment:
What do I notice?  
After thoroughly reviewing the graph, I have noticed that periods of wet soil are almost always followed by periods of dry soil in the Southwest. 

What do I wonder? 
One thing this graph is making me wonder is if this pattern will always continue. Also, these dates and data are not completely up to date. So, after looking at the graph, I wonder if this data was taken more recently, would it be different? How will climate change affect the data?

What do I think is going on in this graph?  
In this graph, it is displaying the soil wetness or dryness in the Southwest from around the 1500s to the 2000s. It is pulling this data from tree ring width, since wider rings indicate more rain. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
This data relates to me and my community because it points out climate change. Climate change is an issue that will and does affect me and everyone around me. Specifically, the South is an area that produces most of the nation's crops. If droughts continue, this might affect how me and my community get our food.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that the graph changed over time. It started out pretty dry in the beginning, but became less dry in the middle. It also became more dry towards the end of the graph. I also notice that California and Colorado are the driest states in the Southwest. I also notice that that in 2000 it was very wet with hardly any droughts. 

What do you wonder?
What happened in 1572-1600 and currently that made a megadrought? Why was it the wettest right before and right after the megadroughts?

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me because it effects not only the Southwestern part of the United States but also the rest of the United States. We may not all be in a drought. However, the rest of the country is also suffering from being dry. It also shows the effects of climate change not only in the southwest but in all parts of the country.  

What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
In this graph, it shows the moisture in the soil over a period of time and how dry the southwest states are. 
"Soil moisture over time".

raw_comment:
What do I notice?
- I notice that the colors used to indicate whether the soil was dry or wet in the Southwest correspond to common colors for whether soil has moisture or not in real life. Lighter browns usually indicate dryness, while greens indicate well nourished and watered soil through grass. Also, the smaller graph in the corner shows that, since 1520, Nevada and New Mexico have been less dry than California, Arizona, and Colorado. 
What do I wonder?
- What factors caused Nevada and New Mexico to be less dry than California, Colorado, and Arizona, despite being in the same general area? 
- What happened around the eighteenth century that to the soil being particularly wet that year? 
- What factors led to the soil being dry enough around the 1600s and mid-1900s to warrant an orange coloring on the graph? 
What do I think is going on in this graph?
- I think this graph is exhibiting how wet or dry the soil was in the Southwest from 1520 to the 2000s based on rainfall. The small graph in the corner depicts the driest areas of the Southwest in 2000-2001 since 1520. 
How does this relate to you and your community?
- This relates to me since I have lived in the Southwest before--specifically Arizona. The graph in the bottom corner is not at all surprising to me, as it is always incredibly dry and hot. The way the Southwest is effected by rain is basically the polar opposite to how the area my school is in, the Northeast, is.
Headline:
- Rain's Lack of Aim in the Southwest

I wonder how the effect of the rain and the low on rain storage is going to affect the trees and soil.   

This can affect me and my community, because this could happen to us in New Jersey. We can have have too much rain that can affect people driving, or people trying to walk. Not to mention the plants. Too much water can affect the soil that help the plants grow.  The lack of rain can also make an impact on the soil.  

The history of Southwest United States; Effect of rain and drought

raw_comment:
The variations in drought patterns between each century instantly catch my attention. The wet and dry circumstances were very constant from the middle of the 1600s to the late 1900s; there always seemed to be a wet season after a drought.
During the period of 1572–1600, there was a megadrought that set new records. In the Southwest, almost all of the soil was entirely dry. Presently, identical circumstances exist in the Southwest. However, it has been a little over 400 years since the previous severe drought. This prompts me to speculate about the exact causes of the current megadrought. Like the previous drought, I also wonder if this one will endure 30 years. Will the length decrease?

raw_comment:
I immediately notice the fluctuations in drought patterns between each century. From the mid 1600s to the late 1900s, the wet and dry conditions were pretty consistent; after every drought, there seemed to be a wet period. 
There are two outliers in this graph. Between the years of 1572 and 1600, there was a record-breaking megadrought. Almost 100% of the soil in the Southwest was completely dry. Currently, the Southwest is facing these similar conditions. But it has been a little more than 400 years since the last mega drought. This makes me wonder what specific factors have contributed to the current megadrought. I also wonder if this drought will last 30 years—just like the last one. Will it be shorter? Longer? 
This graph is evidence that our climate is changing. This changing climate is affecting our lives, society, and how we function as a community. For instance, the southwest produces more than half of America’s crops. How will this drought affect the farming industry, and America’s consumers? And how has it already?

1. What I noticed about this graph is that there were a total of 2 major droughts that occurred. One was from 1572-1600 and another one is from 2000-present. I also noticed that the wettest points were after the droughts in which there was a spike in soil moisture.

2. What I wonder is that by using this data, can there be a possibility of finding a solution to these droughts? Also, could it be that this current megadrought is causing the spike in wildfires?

3. The way this relates to my community is that this past summer, the state of New Jersey was on drought alert and summer 2022 was the hottest summer recorded since 2016. Also, this past summer here it was very dry to a point where the front lawns and backyards were drying up worse than usual.

4. This graph is showing data that was recorded from thousands of years ago to the present time regarding soil moisture which is causing droughts.

from my class:

We were thinking about the impact on our community in terms of farming and talking about how vertical farming might become more popular since it uses less water.  We also had a conversation about what might be causing the current dryness and how it can be slowed/stopped (electric vehicles came up). This graph is showing the soil moisture percentage from 1500- the present day. It shows the previous megadrought of 1572-1600 and the Southwest is entering another megadrought. I noticed that from 1800 to the late 1900s, the soil moisture percentile remained around the same. I also noticed that even after the megadrought from 1572-1600, there was still a high peak of dry soil. I wonder what factors affect the megadroughts occurring and why they are not very common. This relates to my community because as the Southwest enters another megadrought, it may affect other aspects of the entire country.

This means that certain types of produce may not be in the grocery stores this fall and if they are the prices will probably be higher than before. It also means people might start moving away from the Southwest and to the East coast which can cause house prices here to inflate even more. "Droughts in the Southwest: Some of the Worst in History"

The first thing that caught my attention about this graph was the severity of the mega drought in the years 1572-1600. Within this time frame virtually the entire southwest had less than 25% moisture. I can assume that the average soil moisture percentage expected in the southwest is less than 75% and greater than 25%. I also noticed that after an extreme soil moisture trend there tends to be another extreme trend. For example after the mega drought a majority of the soul had over 75% moisture. Before the current mega drought there was a period where the entire soil moisture was over 75%.

I wonder what caused the entirety of the soil moisture percentage around the year 2000 to be over 75% moisture.

Through documenting these trends of moisture the creators of the graph are also displaying the changing in extreme weather patterns.

Through displaying the changing weather patterns this graph is showing the prevalence of climate change in the extreme fluctuations. Even though this graph only shows the Southwest, the issue of climate change is one that effects everyone, no matter the location.

raw_comment:
This graph displays the past droughts in the south from the 1500s to now. I notice that there is much less green in the graph, signifying less moisture and more drought throughout the years. I also notice that during the years there is green it is never over 100% of the land. 
I wonder why before there is a major drought there appears to be the a lot of green before then. 
This relates to me and my community because it is concerning that the Southwest is entering into their driest drought since 1520. Global warming has become a big issue and it is clearly shown by this graph. Global warming is worse in some areas, like the south, and it is important to be aware of it and try to help out. 
Headline: 
The Evolution of the Fried Southwest

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
The Southwest experienced waves of dry and wet periods. It seems that the driest periods were squished between two very wet periods. In the 1500-1700, there seems to be more consistent change between wet and dry periods. While going to the 1700-1900, there are consistent droughts. 

What do you wonder?
There was a megadrought during 1572-1600 and a current mega drought. I wonder what the causes of these mega droughts are. The current drought would likely be a cause of climate change, but what could have caused it during the 1600. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
The Southwest is often subject to wildfires because of these extreme droughts. Global warming is a current issue that is affecting the world, and the droughts and wildfires are issues that need to be solved. Although my community is not affected by drought, this graph shows that we must find solutions to droughts especially if the megadrought continues. 

What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
The Sun-Baked Southwest - Bring the Moisture Back

I noticed that there was an extreme drought in the years 1572-1600s. There seems to be a similar extreme drought that reoccured in the 2000s as well.

I wonder how human being adapted to these large droughts for such long periods of time. Especially those who may have never experienced or even heard of a drought before. 

3. How does this relate to me and my community? 
As I live in NJ there have not experienced a drought in an extreme manner. However this summer we did go through a brief drought and it was a learning experience.

raw_comment: In this graph, we are shown the history of droughts in the Southwest region. A megadrought occurred from 1572-1600, lasting for 28 years. The soil mositure during that drought was incredibly dry, and water was most likely scarce. But for three centuries after that, the droughts stayed calm. Until, suddenly they weren't, and the issues of global warming increased and we are now experiencing a megadrought in the Southwest. But how? How did it stay so calm during that time period? As our world began to warm up, and issues of climate change got larger and larger, how did it not dry out? Living in the South, you expect to experience things like severe heat, but a drought causes things more than just dryness. A drought causes shortages of water, and water of poor quality. A long-lasting drought could cause water scarcity. Communites in the Southwest will experience water scarcity if this drought continues for a long period of time. Once again, this graph shows the history of droughts in the Southwest. And to conclude, my headline for this graph is, "So dry the birds are making barbed wire nests!"

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph displays the soil moisture levels for land in six southwestern U. S. states over the past 500 years.  This information is based on examining the characteristics of tree rings – the field of dendrochronology, on very old trees.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?”, “What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these graphs. We look forward to replying to your discoveries.

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the online article that included this graph plus other Serena graphs.  

Note that you can get a link to your response (and replies made to it) to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, September 23 with moderation on Wednesday, September 28.  The topic – Americans Moving.  Keep noticing and wondering.

raw_comment:
I notice that from 1572-1600, there was a megadrought where the Southwest was the driest it has ever been. From around 1700-1800, the moisture levels rose and stayed around 60-70% until 2000-today when there is another significant drought.

I wonder what the cause of these droughts is, how the region recovered from these droughts, and how they handle the droughts when they are in it.

This relates to my community because climate change has become a very prevalent issue in modern times. This relates to me personally because I am looking at colleges in the Southwest and need to be aware of current issues. 

This graph is showing the droughts that have occurred in the southwest over the past 500-some years

3. How does this relate to you and your community?
This will relate to my community and me because we are the ones currently living in it.  Farms are being affected by it.  It also shows us signs of the current global warming problems.  We are gonna have to find ways to overcome this megadrought.

4. What’s going on in this graph?

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
This graph, in regards to the influence of rain and drought. This course of climate presents a variety of moisture stages over the course of nearly 500 years. In present time (2000s), the rate of droughts have further increased, something that was last seen in 1572-1600.  
2) What do you wonder?
I wonder, what was the initial purpose of such graph. Be it general awareness, or apart of a bigger picture. As for the way it was conveyed, why would the rates/effects of rain and drought be illustrated as such rather than presented with more numerical data. Hence, taking a more statistical approach. Furthermore, does this assists others that part take in a climate related field in understanding or resolving the decline in aggressive climate change?
3) How does this relate to you and your community?
The environment in which we reside in is greatly influenced by such instances of rain and droughts. The droughts have a particular influence in which it's affect on the environment create conditions that create difficulty for farming and promote spread of illness and disease. 
4) What´s going on in this graph? Create a headline
This graph sums up the influence of rain and droughts in the span of 500 or so years. 
Headline: A break in historic record, the megadrought strikes again!

I notice ... the towering, erupting volcano that is the megadrought.

I wonder... Is it a megadrought because it lasted 30 years, or is it a megdrought because of how dry it was. And if it's the latter, are we approaching that again?
I don't really think it does. I mean I don't have a group and I'm too anixous to actually go and join anyone, so solo speedrun go brr.

Like climate change is happening and the graph shows how much worse the droughts have been getting, but beyond that I wouldn't say if it directly affects me. One of my friends has family in California, but I don't remember if it's NorCal or SoCal. They might be at Berkley? I dunno. 

I mean climate change and everything to do with that has everything to do with everyone. I dunno. It's such a grand scale of things so I can't really wrap my head around it.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I see that the majority of the land has historically fallen between the 25th and 75th percentiles for soil moisture. The land never stays the same and the soil moisture always seems to fluctuate between high and low percentiles, yet occasionally it does resemble a previous period. Additionally, I see that the majority of the land is in the 75th to 95th percentile both before and after the megadrought.
What do you wonder?
I'm curious as to why megadroughts occur and whether this is a normal occurrence. I wonder whether there is anything we can do to stop this from getting worse and if global warming is to blame for this. If global warming is to blame for these droughts, how will it affect them? Will it make them worse, happen faster, or continue longer?
How does this relate to you and your community?
My community is affected because we are the primary source of climate change. Our failure to care for the earth as we should is demonstrated by the significant changes in the environment. This may harm both people's agriculture and communities. Due to the drought levels, mass production may be delayed.
What’s going on in this graph?
SouthWest has dried up!

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that at certain dry areas there are orange lines which indicate a dry period drier than 1520. I also noticed that around the 2000s the soil was very wet and then  it suddenly started to get drier. There was also the megadrought from 1572-1600 and the current one that's happening right now. I also noticed that from 1700-1900 there wasn't a large period of wetness or dryness.
What do you wonder?
I wonder why a mega drought happened so soon after what was the wettest period recorded according to the graph.  I also wonder why there wasn't a large amount of wetness or dryness from 1700-1900 when every other period seems to either be very wet or very dry. It's also intriguing how there's data that goes back several hundred years from now, who obtained all this data and how did they do it?
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to not just me and my community, but the whole world. Global warming results in unpredictable weather like what's shown in the graph with the soil having a lot of moisture and then suddenly becoming very dry in the early 2000s. For example, two years ago it was snowing in October which only ever happened back in the 90's. This data shows the effects of global warming and everyone can feel its effects one way or another, whether it's in the southwest or the northeast.
What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
Soil in the Southwest ain't feeling so wet

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
- I notice that most of the land over the years has been between the 25th-75th soil moisture percentile. The soil moisture always seems to change between high and low percentiles, the land never stays the same, but it sometimes does look similar to a time before it. Also, I notice that before and after the megadrought most of the land is in the 75th to 95th percentile.

What do you wonder? 
- I wonder why megadroughts happen and is it natural for this to happen. I wonder if there are ways we can prevent this from becoming worse and could this be happening because of global warming. If global warming is the cause of these droughts how does it affect it, does it make the droughts worse, does it speed them up or make them last longer.

How does this relate to you and your community? 
- This relates to me and my community because these megadroughts could affect many crops and people's food. Even though these droughts don't really affect us, but they affect other families and we need to help out. Also, if global warming is causing these droughts we are the problem because we don't take care of our environment enough. 

What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
- The graph shows the soil moisture percentile throughout the years in the southwest and when megadroughts have happened.
"The Southwest Dries Up"

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

I noticed that there was a grace period between the early 1700s to the mid 1900s where the droughts were not as inferior. I also noticed the quickly increasing spike of dry soil becoming present in the current mega drought.

What do you wonder?

I wonder if the soil moisture being at an all time high in the early 2000s had something to do with the upcoming megadrought. Was this a calm before the storm. I also wonder what caused all the moisture in the soil to be taken aback so quickly.

How does this relate to you and your community?

This relates to my community due to the differences in weather the past few years. New Jersey has been notorious for its drought season recently with it being at a D2 during drought season.  By seeing these changes one can relate the southwest's droughts and grace periods of moisture to NJs recently.
 
What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

This graph is showing the drastic changes in soil moisture and how what once can be in the 95th percentile can quickly decrease into the 5th in the following year. 
Catchy title : 
"Droughts drown the Southwest in attempt to regain the megadrought title"

| Areas marked “Driest since 1520” (2000–2021) | Categorical/nominal | Orange highlight color on inset map |
raw_comment:
1) The Southwest is normally somewhat dry. The Southwest is currently experiencing a megadrought, the driest it has been since the 1600. In 1572, the Southwest previously experienced a megadrought, which lasted through the 1600. Before the Southwest began to go through its second megadrought last since 1600, the Southwest was wettest it has ever been.
2) Before the Southwest entered its second megadrought, why did the Southwest become the wettest it has ever been? That has never happened before when it’s about to experience a megadrought.
3) Like the Southwest, the central part of New Jersey has also been experiencing severe drought the past months. Similar to the Southwest, the drought has been negatively affecting our air quality, sanitation, and hygiene. Sooner or later, we will be seeing more places in New Jersey and other states experiencing drier weather due to climate change.
4) The graph shows the moisture of the Southwest over the past centuries. A catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea is “Warlike Climate Change: The Endless Withering of the Southwest”!

3.) How does it affect us and our community?  We live in a heavy agricultural community.  Soil moisture affects our farmers' abilities to grow their crops and feed their livestock.  
4.) Catchy title?  "The dry tides of drought"

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

I observe that between the years the graph has given us, between 1500 and 1600, the land was the driest it has ever been. It's been the wettest year ever, just like it was in 2000. Additionally, I've found that the land was at its best between 1700 and 1800 because it was neutrally dry and moist at the same time. Last but not least, I've also come to the realization that between the years 2020–2021, there were only two tiny patches of neutral land, and the rest were extremely dry.

What do you wonder?

After all the many types of weather the land has experienced, I wonder if this is a result of climate change, if the land would ever attain the ideal soil moisture, and if that would actually be best for the land.


How does this relate to you and your community?

This is relevant to my community because, while not being from the South, it is a part of where I reside. It is important to understand both the positive and negative aspects of the world, including its climate. Especially knowing that at any moment it can affect my community. 


What’s going on in this graph? 

The graph displays the amount of soil moisture from the beginning of life up until the year 2021.


Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
A rising issue: Southwest Soil Moisture influenced by climate change

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that before and after a big drought, there is always a lot of moisture in the soil. The graph constantly fluctuates between high moisture and low moisture. Additionally, the severity of the drought and the amount of moisture have increased drastically since the 1900s. The last time period with similar severity to today was from 1550 to 1700. The incoming megadrought is most likely going to be very severe, and we've already seen its effects in places like California with the ongoing wildfires.

2. I wonder if this process is natural. If so, how much has global warming affected it? Did global warming speed up or increase the severity of the megadroughts? Following the patterns in the graph, is it possible to estimate when the next megadroughts will come, and how long and severe they will be? Can these estimations (knowing when the droughts will come) help us prevent them?

3. This relates to my community because my generation will be the one that has to deal with the current megadrought, along with the environmental issues which will follow it. Food supply from farms and living conditions in the Southwest will decrease and worsen more as the drought continues. 

4. The graph shows us soil moisture percentiles since the 1500s, from which we can derive the time periods where there were droughts or a lot of moisture. My headline is "Climate Change: Erasing Doubt through Drought."

   - There is **no faceting** or small multiples in the main chart.
   - A **map inset** on the right provides geographic context for the highlighted recent period.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / time period | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Percent of land | Quantitative | Position on y-axis / total stacked height |
| Soil moisture percentile category | Ordinal | Color/hue of stacked bands |
| Megadrought period annotation (e.g., 1572–1600, Current megadrought) | Temporal | Text labels and bracket annotations above chart |
| Region / state (Calif., Nev., Utah, Ariz., Colo., N.M.) | Categorical/nominal | Position in inset map and text labels |
| Areas marked “Driest since 1520” (2000–2021) | Categorical/nominal | Orange highlight color on inset map |

raw_comment:
1. This graph shows the climate change in the Southwest of the United States over the past 500 years. It shows the amount of data collected on the concentration of soil moisture to its driest all the way to its wettest point. I seemed to have noticed two major details on this graph, through the time period 1572-1600 was known to be called a megadrought point. Practically its highest drought point. The year 2000 shows a similar look but instead it shows its wettest point and actually seems to be the highest. 

2. I wonder if the data they've collected could help them manage to figure out a solution to solve the drought problems. And I'm also curious if they're only focusing on the drought problem in the Southwest.

3. This relates to me and my community because this can negatively affect people's crops and also hurt communities.This can slow down mass production due to the drought levels.

4. Southwest's Drought Problem

Also, since 1520, some of Cali, Colorado, and Arizona were the driest. Lastly, from 1700-1800, the soil moisture was mainly between the 25th and the 75th.

What do you notice?

I noticed there are various amounts of brown spikes throughout the years which represents dry soil, it has been the driest in 2000-2021 since 1572-1600.

What do you wonder? 

I wonder what factors played into the dry soil spikes and what can people in America do to ensure the soil becomes more moist.

How does this relate to you and your community? 

This relates to me and my community because I live in a country where states are in droughts. People living in other states need to find ways to conserve water and cant even tend to their basic needs. Although I don't live in a state like that it still effects me and if this problem gets worse it can spread throughout the country.  

What is going on in the graph? 

The graph consists of a timeline that documents the peaks of when the soil was the driest compare to when it was the wettest. 

Headline

No Sprouts During A Megadrought

raw_comment:
1. What I notice in this graph is how there is mainly moderate soil moisture when it comes to the percentage of land. I also notice how when the driest soil moisture levels are hit, they hit with a very steep slope but do not last for that long. Go big or go home.

2. When I look at this graph, I wonder how these droughts can leave such a massive impact in a short amount of time, and when would the grace period be before droughts occur.

3. This relates to the community because people tend to face natural shortages as a result of drought, and the sad part is we never see it coming. Droughts can impact the water supply and a way of living if there are no resources, so being able to maintain soil moisture levels could benefit the community.

4. What's going on in this graph is we are seeing the soil moisture levels over the last 500 years and how this might affect people in the Southwest. I would call this graph, "I Drought The Southwest Can Ever Catch a Break: History Of The Southwestern Droughts."

What do you notice?
1) I noticed that in the year 2000, the green, which is the wettest soil, reached its all-time high. This signifies a surplus in rain and moisture that previously had not appeared. 

What do you wonder?
2) Since the graph shows it has never reached this level of green before, does this new weather have anything to do with the growing effects of climate change?

How does this relate to you and your community?
3)This relates to me and my community because if the weather is changing in other places like it previously hasn't then climate change can also affect my surrounding areas/soil as well.

What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline. 
4)In this graph we see how the levels of soil moisture are increasing throughout the years. This is most likely due to weather changes and an increase in rain possibly due to climate change. A headline for this can be; "Southwest Soil Moisture Quickening with Climate Change."

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice? 

I notice that most soil moisture has been around the 25 to 75th percentile. I also notice that there will be megadroughts on the years 1572-1600 and 2000-2002. During each century, around 50% of the land would be dry. 

2. What do you wonder?

I wonder what effects the drought had in the 1572-1600 for people and the plants. I want to know how people made the best of the situation although the soil was really dry. I also wonder what people in the Southwest would do if the soil moisture was really wet. 

3. How does this relate to you and your community? 

This relates to me and my community because this is an example of what could happen anywhere at any time because of climate change. This could affect a lot of things like production of prodict and it becoming scarce. So, it is good to be able to see a visual of what all of Earth could be. 

4. What's going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline. 

In this graph, the soil moisture in the Southwest would go through many of stages from being the driest to being the wettest in the past 500 years because of climate change. A catchy headline would be: "Climate change: How it affected Southwest Soil".

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed straight off the bat that we're in a current megadrought. Also during the 1700s and 1800's there was significantly more beige. Then the only other megadrought was during 1572-1600 where the graph shows the biggest spike. 
What do you wonder?
I wonder what other factors play into this. Obviously climate change but what other factors play into this. I'd assume the location due to the Southwest being known for it's dry climate.

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and I since it's our world that is undergoing the drought. It's our future that's doomed if the drought doesn't get any better. As humans, we are programmed to require water and a water source but without water how will we see that future?

What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
This graph shows how the water in the Southwest has a common pattern of disappearing. If it's in history, what's stopping another megadrought to happen again? The catchy title I'd use for this graph is "What happened to the water in the Southwest?"

raw_comment:
1) I found that there was a megadrought in the 1600s, specifically in the driest percentiles that can be detected, the 5th and 25th percentiles, during the years 1572-1600. The data was entered into what appears to be a climograph that shows data for temperature and precipitation. This can illustrate that when the drought becomes drier, less precipitation can be anticipated. A 25 percentile drought that predominantly affected roughly 50–60% of the area occurred between the years 1750 and 1980. 

2) I wonder if climatologists are trying to find a solution to the mega-drought that is currently happening in the southwest regions? Has this affected the agriculture of mass food-producing states? Does human interference have any contribution to this sudden change in climate?

3) This graph relates to my community in El Salvador. Around 50% of the people in Guatemala, Nicaragua, Honduras, and El Salvador are affected by the accumulation of heat brought on by climate change, which has left their crops devastated and left 7 million people in Latin America without enough natural resources for their agriculture, making it difficult to find food. Climate has also caused a drop in livestock in both the U.S and E.S which comes to show that these effects need to be stopped in order to replenish our resources. 

4) I would give the graph the title "MEGA DROUGHT: Effects of Climate Change Experienced Throughout the Globe is Showing its Unmerciful Impact On the SouthWest"

1. In this chart I noticed that the highest droughts have either ended with the wettest land or started off with the wettest land. There was a megadrought from 1572-1600 and just now the southwest is currently going through a megadrought.

2. I wonder if climatologist have had any progress on finding a solution to the issue of droughts or if they have had any conclusion on how to control the oncurring issue of the drought in the southwest.

3. This relates to my community because I come from a country that has dealt with a drought before. Usually when a drought occurs in a country, the crops face a massive drop in production since the soil is dry. Mexico in 1996 had one of the worst droughts on record and the country suffered a huge crop loss. Even today, nearly 85% of the country is currently facing dry weather conditions. This causes a problem for the people as they have less crops to produce and it progressively gets difficult to get fresh products to eat or sell.

4. This graph is showing the soil conditions in the southwest over decades where droughts have been recorded along with times it's rained the most. My headline would be " The Southwest and its Withered Conditions Through the Sands of Time".

|---|---|---|

raw_comment:
1. I notice that after a megadrought there is an increasing amount of wetness that follows and vice versa. Also, between the years 1700 to 1800, the soil percentage stayed between the 25th and 75th. 

2. Does the mega-drought or the dramatic increase in wetness have anything to do with human interference in the climate such as an increase in industrialization? 

3. I think this relates to my community because dramatic climate change in other parts of the country can result in changes near my country. Also, where this climate was affected were states such as California which happen to import products to other parts of the US such as fruits, vegetables, nuts, and, personally for me, hair products. 

4. This graph is showing the history of drought in the Southwest. My headline would be "Climates Decades-long Time Span In the Southwest".

raw_comment:
I notice that this graph relates to the cumulative effects of rain and drought in the Southwest for over five centuries. I notice that the percentiles of soil moisture (from driest and wettest) have varied throughout the years. I notice that over the years there has been more rain and soil moisture. But I also notice there seems to be a current megadrought. I notice that from certain areas in California, Utah, Colorado, and Arizona have been the most affected and driest since 1520. 

I wonder what other factors have affected (both positively and negatively) drought in the Southwest. I wonder how exactly these droughts have affected these areas (with agriculture and more). I wonder if the government has tried to do anything to help improve the situation in the driest locations. 

I believe that this relates to me and my community because I assume these droughts cause effects that not only affect those who live in the affected areas but also the nation. I mean this can cause problems with water shortage, and as humans we need water to survive. Also, I feel as if this would take a toll on crops and agriculture, and obviously goods are shipped from different locations. So this could possible take a toll on my community’s nutrition and alimentation. But as we have seen, mostly there has been more soil moisture throughout the years, which is extremely important and beneficial.

Droughts of the Southwest: A Timeline of Triumph and Failure

raw_comment:
1.) What do you notice?
One thing that really stuck out to me was during the time period from 1572 through 1600, almost 100% of the Southwest was experiencing the driest amount of land ever, classifying this time period as a "megadrought".

2.) What do you wonder?
I wonder why there was a decline in dryness around the 1700s and up until early 2000? Why was the land wetter during this time frame in comparison to the "megadrought" time period? Would environmentalists consider these past two decades a dry time period for the Southwestern states or not?

3.) What impact does this have on you and your community?
This graph proves how different regions in the United States are left with a low amount of natural resources that their lives rely on. This also is a dangerous factor because the limiting amount of water these states have can also lead to natural disasters.

4.) What is going on in this graph?
This graph shows the effects that rain has on the Southwest region of the United States from before the 1500s through the 2000s and more recently.

Catchline: Dust Bowl of the Southwest.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed a pattern in the centurial soil moisture percentiles. Whenever there would be a period of dryness, then it would tend to be followed by an equally moist period. 

2. I wonder why the 1700s were so much less dry compared to every other time period? Perhaps that was the result of a negative environmental feedback loop? And if so, then what would be the exact causes? 

3. I do not live in the Southwest, so this graph doesn't directly effect me. But I do worry that Global Warming will eventually lead to everywhere in the U.S. experiencing a megadrought, or even just as consistently dry conditions as the Southwest in recent centuries. 

4. "The Patterns of Soil Moisture in the Southwest"

1. What do you notice?
I notice that there have been many droughts since the year 1500. It seems like there is constantly a drought and the majority of the time, the soil is very dry as opposed to the minority of the time where the soil is wet. I also notice that we are currently in one of the biggest mega droughts since 1500.

A headline for this graph could be "The Changes of Soil Over the Years".
